title: IB English A: Language & Literature
description: Explore how literary and non-literary texts shape ideas about culture, identity and power—and how those influences shape language in turn. Develop your analysis through close reading of different text types.

items.title: Reading words and images
items.summary: How do verbal and visual choices shape our response?
items.body:
## Our guiding question
How do verbal and visual choices shape our response?

## Read and notice
Bring a passage or image from your current class text. Make three observations about the choices its creator has made.

## Discuss
- Which detail most strongly shapes your response?
- How might another reader interpret it differently?
- What evidence helps you explain your reading?

## Make your thinking visible
Try the close reading lab, then use the paragraph workshop to turn one interpretation into a developed response.

items.title: From observation to analysis
items.summary: Connect evidence to meaning, with a worked example and interactive magic-sentence workshop.
items.body:
## Start with a precise observation
What word, image, pattern, or structural choice catches your attention? Quote briefly and accurately.

## Explore a possible effect
How might that choice shape a reader’s response? Consider the context before making a claim about its effect.

## Connect detail to meaning
Explain how the evidence supports your interpretation. A useful starting phrase is: “This choice suggests … because …”

## Test your interpretation
Can you find a second detail that supports your reading? Is there evidence that complicates it? Revise your idea if necessary.

items.title: Paper 1
items.summary: Analyse how verbal and visual choices in a previously unseen non-literary text create meaning.
items.imageAlt: An engraving representing optics, with an eye in a star and figures holding optical instruments.
items.imageCredit: An eye in a star representing optics · Wellcome Collection
items.body:
## Briefing

Paper 1 is a guided analysis of previously unseen non-literary material. The guiding question gives you a productive way into the text: use it to build a focused interpretation rather than attempting to catalogue everything you notice.

SL students choose one of the two texts. HL students analyse both. In either case, the central job is the same: explain how deliberate choices shape meaning for a particular audience and purpose.

> **First principle:** establish what the text is doing as a whole before examining individual details. Technique only matters when it helps explain that larger purpose.

## Method

[Unpack the guiding question](/resources/unpacking-questions#paper-1) before selecting your evidence.


[Writing an introduction: step-by-step guidance and a worked example](/resources/paper-1-introductions?example=language-literature)

### 1. Orient

- Read the contextual information and identify the text type, creator, audience, purpose, and situation.
- Record your first response. What seems urgent, unsettling, persuasive, intimate, comic, or controlled?
- Read the guiding question closely. Put what it asks you to analyse into your own words.

### 2. Survey

- Divide the text into meaningful sections and note shifts in tone, argument, focus, scale, or visual emphasis.
- Identify the overall movement of the text before concentrating on isolated devices.
- For multimodal texts—those combining forms such as words and images—trace the relationship between words, image, layout, typography, framing, and sequence.
- If the text is an infographic, consult the [Infographic guide](/courses/language-literature/text-types/c1e54cf5-1489-440b-a98c-3e7107bacc62) for questions about hierarchy, scale, labels and source.
- For commercial advertising, use the [Advertisement guide](/courses/language-literature/text-types/cf482e4c-3555-4e12-afca-b63396aec3ea) and its separate FIJI Water example to examine appeals, product claims and visual contrast.

- For fundraising, use the [Charitable appeal guide](/courses/language-literature/text-types/b0a0e8bb-7dfb-4fd6-8da0-a19d3dc95e92) and its WWF adoption example to connect need, trust and participation.

### 3. Select

- Choose patterns and details that directly support your interpretation.
- Prefer brief, precise evidence over long quotations or inventories of techniques.
- Ask what each choice does, why it suits this audience and purpose, and how it contributes to the text as a whole.

### 4. Construct

- State a focused thesis that answers the guiding question and offers an interpretation.
- Organize paragraphs around ideas or effects. Do not organize the essay as a tour of devices.
- Move from evidence to choice, effect, and significance. A useful test is: **what does this detail help the creator make the audience think, feel, notice, or accept?**

### 5. Verify

- Check that every paragraph advances the thesis.
- Remove claims that the evidence cannot support.
- Proofread for precise vocabulary, integrated quotations, sentence control, and clear transitions.

### Need another way in?

If the initial method leaves you unsure where to begin, try [SOAPSTone](/courses/language-literature/resources/eab78d37-cc35-476e-a70b-d1b674c8f512): Speaker, Occasion, Audience, Purpose, Subject, and Tone. It gives you prompts for an initial rhetorical reading; use the resulting observations to build your argument.

For poetry in Literature, [TPCASTT](/courses/literature/resources/81a5570b-6369-4557-b98b-9d8fa1be2f52) offers a different scaffold. Choose the tool that suits the text. Neither framework is a required essay structure.

## Avoid

Use this as a quick diagnosis when a response is not working.

### Interpretation problems

- Retelling the content without interpreting its significance.
- Making broad claims about symbolism without considering context.
- Discussing only the “big picture” or only tiny details, rather than connecting the two.
- Selecting evidence that is interesting but unrelated to the guiding question.

### Analysis problems

- Naming a device and stopping there.
- Using effects that could apply to almost any text: “grabs attention,” “creates an image,” or “makes the reader want to read on.”
- Treating every feature separately instead of noticing patterns and combinations.
- Assuming the creator’s intention when the text itself does not support the claim.

### Organization problems

- Beginning without a defensible thesis or clear line of inquiry.
- Organizing paragraphs by device instead of by an interpretive idea.
- Starting body paragraphs with line references or quotations before establishing the point.
- Repeating the introduction in the conclusion instead of explaining the larger significance of the reading.

## Criteria

### A · Understanding and interpretation

**What is the text communicating?** Show that you understand both its literal meaning and its larger implications. Develop a convincing interpretation and support it with well-chosen references. A textual reference can be a quotation or another precise reference to the text.

### B · Analysis and evaluation

**How does the text communicate it?** Explain how textual features and authorial choices create meaning. Evaluation means showing how and why those choices work within this particular text. Precise terminology can help, but naming a technique never substitutes for developed analysis.

### C · Focus and organization

Establish a clear line of argument, develop it logically, and keep every paragraph relevant to the guiding question. There is no single required structure. Context belongs only where it advances the interpretation rather than interrupting it.

### D · Language

Communicate the analysis clearly with precise, varied, and appropriately formal language. Aim for control rather than ornate jargon. Integrate evidence smoothly and leave time to correct errors that interrupt meaning.

## Practice

Use short, repeatable drills before attempting another full paper:

1. **Five-minute orientation:** identify audience, purpose, text type, context, and first impression.
2. **Guiding-question rewrite:** express the question as a direct analytical task in your own words.
3. **Pattern hunt:** find three connected choices and explain the larger effect they create together.
4. **Thesis test:** write a thesis, then underline the part that offers an interpretation rather than a topic.
5. **Paragraph audit:** label the evidence, analytical verb, effect, and larger significance in one paragraph.

[Open Passage Practice](/practice/passages) to work with an unseen text and receive focused feedback on literary analysis.

## Field tools

Use a compact check before revising:

- Is my interpretation supported by precise references?
- Have I explained how choices shape meaning?
- Does each paragraph advance the response to the question?
- Is my language clear and precise?

For additional prompts, open [SOAPSTone](/courses/language-literature/resources/eab78d37-cc35-476e-a70b-d1b674c8f512) or [From observation to analysis](/courses/language-literature/resources/bfa6c8ee-0901-4cc2-b3fb-2070394d9432).

## Models

Explore Becky’s CDC advertisement in the worked-example panel alongside this guidance (below it on smaller screens). Follow the five steps, then open the analytical paragraph to see how a verbal choice and a visual detail support a single interpretation. Try transferring the method to the Amanda or Brian advertisement using the comparison prompts.

items.title: Paper 2
items.summary: Build a comparative argument about two literary works studied in the course.
items.imageAlt: A woodcut of two bookbinders sewing and pressing books.
items.imageCredit: Two bookbinders at work · Wellcome Collection
items.body:
## Briefing

Build a comparative argument about two literary works in response to the chosen question. This guidance applies to both Literature and Language & Literature. Your interpretation should answer the question through the relationship between the works, supported by precise knowledge of their choices.

## Method

[Unpack a Paper 2 question](/resources/unpacking-questions#paper-2), then try an original question from the practice bank.


### Unpack the question
Identify the central concept and the analytical task. Rephrase it as something you can argue about. Keep its particular wording in view as you select the works and evidence.

### Establish a basis for comparison
Find a meaningful relationship: a shared concern handled differently, a similar technique with different effects, or different routes to a comparable outcome. Difference alone is not yet an argument.

### Plan around claims
Write a comparative thesis and two or three supporting claims. For each claim, collect a precise moment from each work and explain how the writers' choices support the comparison. Choose a structure that lets those connections develop clearly.

### Sustain the relationship
Bring each discussion back to the question and the other work. Explain why the similarity or difference matters; a connective such as “similarly” cannot do that thinking for you.

## Avoid

- Two separate essays joined by a brief comparison at the end.
- Retelling events instead of examining how the writers present them.
- A prepared theme essay that only loosely fits the question.
- General claims about historical context that do not illuminate a textual choice.
- Treating balance as an identical word count rather than substantial attention to both works.

## Criteria

### Knowledge and interpretation
Use accurate, specific references and interpret their significance for the question.

### Analysis and comparison
Explain how choices shape meaning, then develop the relationship between the works. The comparison should advance the argument.

### Focus and organization
Make the direction clear and arrange the ideas so each stage develops the response.

### Language
Write precisely and integrate references into your own sentences. These are reading prompts for the criteria; consult the official guide for the full descriptors.

## Practice

1. Write a comparative claim without using the phrase “both texts show.”
2. Pair one moment from each work. Identify a choice, its effect, and the significance of the comparison.
3. Test a plan: can every paragraph answer the exact question?

Use the [paragraph workshop](/courses/language-literature/practice/58896b5a-8853-48e4-9298-a8f6d64d0863) to develop one claim before drafting a full essay.

## Field tools

Make a compact planning grid: **claim · evidence from work A · evidence from work B · choices · significance of the comparison**. Fill it in before choosing paragraph order.

Return to [From observation to analysis](/courses/language-literature/resources/bfa6c8ee-0901-4cc2-b3fb-2070394d9432) when evidence is doing more describing than explaining.

## Models

### A useful comparative claim
“Although both works present authority as dependent on public performance, one exposes its fragility through interruptions in dialogue while the other reveals it through a narrator's distance.”

This is a structural illustration, not a claim about specified works. It identifies a relationship and distinct authorial choices; it still needs precise evidence and adjustment to the question.

items.title: Individual Oral
items.summary: Explore how a global issue is presented through close analysis and connections to the wider works.
items.imageAlt: An engraving showing a camera obscura in use in a landscape and as a technical diagram.
items.imageCredit: A camera obscura shown in use and in diagram · Wellcome Collection
items.body:
## Briefing

Explore how a global issue is presented through close analysis and discussion of the wider works.

**Language & Literature:** a literary work and a non-literary body of work.

**Literature:** two literary works, one originally written in English and one studied in translation.

The preparation principles below apply to both. Keep the relevant course's text-selection requirements in view.

## Method

### Focus the issue
Formulate an issue precise enough to analyse and broad enough to matter beyond a single text. Test whether both selections offer substantial evidence of its presentation.

### Select the extracts
Choose passages with significant authorial choices. An extract should give you opportunities for close analysis and meaningful connections beyond its boundaries.

### Move between close and wide
For each selection, explain how particular details present the issue, then connect them to the wider work or body of work. Plan those connections explicitly.

### Rehearse an argument
Use concise prompts to sustain a clear line of thought. Practise transitions and balanced attention; listen for places where you describe content instead of analysing choices.

## Avoid

- Delivering a speech about the issue with the texts used as illustrations.
- Analysing techniques without returning to the issue.
- Staying inside the extracts and neglecting the wider works.
- Making broad claims about the wider work without specific references.
- Reading a script instead of developing a controlled oral explanation.

## Criteria

### A · Knowledge, understanding and interpretation
Support an interpretation of the texts in relation to the global issue with precise references.

### B · Analysis and evaluation
Explain how the creators' choices present the issue, in both the extracts and the wider works.

### C · Focus and organization
Maintain a coherent line of thought and give substantial attention to both selections.

### D · Language
Speak clearly and accurately with language suited to analytical discussion.

## Practice

Give a one-minute explanation that connects one choice to the global issue. Then add a specific connection to the wider work.

Record a rehearsal and identify one passage that merely describes content. Replace it with an explanation of how a choice shapes meaning.

## Field tools

Use a preparation grid with five columns: **detail · choice · effect · relation to the global issue · wider-work connection**.

Return to [From observation to analysis](/courses/language-literature/resources/bfa6c8ee-0901-4cc2-b3fb-2070394d9432) to check the analytical steps in each example.

## Models

### A connection to develop
“In the extract, [specific choice] presents the issue as […]. Elsewhere in the work, [precise moment] develops or complicates this through […].”

The second example should extend the interpretation. Merely stating that the issue occurs elsewhere does not explain how the writer presents it.

items.title: SOAPSTone: a rhetorical reading scaffold
items.summary: A second way into speeches, advertisements, and other rhetorical texts.
items.body:
## When to use it
If you are unsure where to begin with a persuasive text, use these six prompts to gather initial observations. Select the observations that help answer the guiding question; the acronym is a reading aid, not an essay structure.

## The six prompts
- **Speaker:** who speaks, and whose authority or experience does the text draw on? Distinguish a quoted voice from the organization publishing it.
- **Occasion:** what situation gives the text its purpose? Use supplied context and textual evidence; leave unknown details unknown.
- **Audience:** who is addressed? Identify clues in language, images, assumed knowledge, and the action requested.
- **Purpose:** what does the text invite that audience to think, feel, or do?
- **Subject:** what is it about at the literal level? Keep this distinct from its persuasive purpose.
- **Tone:** what attitude comes through, and where does it change? Support your description with particular choices.

## Turn notes into analysis
For the CDC Becky advertisement, distinguish the CDC as publisher from Becky as the personal voice. Then connect the warning tone of the headline with the encouraging offer of help. Explain why that movement might matter to a smoker considering quitting.

Choose two or three connected observations and develop an interpretation. Avoid writing six disconnected paragraphs simply to complete the acronym.

items.title: Infographic
items.summary: How infographics combine information, design and persuasion, with a worked public-health example.
items.body:
## What is an infographic?

An infographic communicates information through a deliberate combination of words, images and layout. It can make a complex idea easier to grasp, organise information for quick reference, or make an argument appear clear and compelling. Some contain charts and statistics; others explain a process or give instructions without plotting any data.

Read it as a complete text. A number, icon or colour acquires meaning through its relationship with the surrounding words and design.

## Uses and purposes

- **Explain:** turn a process, system or unfamiliar concept into labelled stages, diagrams or examples.
- **Inform:** summarise research, report a situation or give readers information they can retrieve quickly.
- **Compare:** align alternatives, changes over time or differences between groups.
- **Persuade:** select and arrange information to support a position, raise concern or encourage a decision.
- **Guide action:** translate advice into steps, targets, precautions or practical choices.

Purposes often overlap. A charity may use statistics to inform readers while encouraging donations; a public-health organisation may explain a risk while promoting a behaviour. Identify the particular combination rather than assuming that every infographic is neutral information.

## Common features and techniques

### Headline and framing claim

What is presented as the main finding or problem?

**Possible analysis:** The headline can give the details a preferred interpretation. Check whether the evidence supports its wording.

### Visual hierarchy and salience

What stands out through scale, contrast, position or white space?

**Possible analysis:** Prominence can prioritise a fact or instruction. Explain why that element matters to the message.

### Layout and reading path

How do columns, panels, arrows or numbering connect ideas?

**Possible analysis:** Arrangement may suggest sequence, comparison or cause and effect. Those relationships still need scrutiny.

### Icons, pictograms and illustrations

What do images represent, simplify or leave out?

**Possible analysis:** Familiar images can make an abstract idea easier to recognise, but may also oversimplify a complex issue.

### Labels and anchorage

How do words direct the interpretation of an image or number?

**Possible analysis:** A label can narrow an image's meanings; a qualification—a limit or condition—can change what a prominent figure means.

### Colour and typography

How are elements grouped, distinguished or emphasised?

**Possible analysis:** Establish the practical relationship before claiming a symbolic effect. Colour associations depend on context.

### Numbers and data displays

Are figures measurements, recommendations, comparisons or estimates?

**Possible analysis:** Numerical precision may lend authority. Check units, scales, denominators and qualifications where applicable.

### Sources and institutional identity

Who publishes the text, and whose evidence does it use?

**Possible analysis:** Logos and source lines may establish credibility, but do not independently prove a claim.

### Calls to action

What is the reader asked to do next?

**Possible analysis:** Imperatives, links or targets may turn understanding into a proposed action.

These are common possibilities, not requirements. Do not invent a chart, axis or legend where the text has none.

## Audience and appeal

Start with **who needs this information and who can act on it**. The people pictured or discussed are not necessarily the intended readers. Support your inference through vocabulary, assumed knowledge, publication context, examples and the action requested.

Then ask what the audience is being offered:

- **Usefulness and accessibility:** brief labels, familiar examples and clear grouping can reduce the effort of finding or applying information.
- **Reason and evidence:** comparisons, quantities and explanations may make a claim appear well supported. Examine the reasoning as well as the appearance of precision.
- **Credibility:** named sources, professional language and institutional identity can invite trust. Consider whether the authority is relevant to this claim.
- **Emotion and values:** depictions of risk, wellbeing, fairness or belonging may connect the information to concerns the audience recognises.
- **Achievable action:** practical steps or a choice of actions can help readers see how they could follow the advice.

Turn the audience inference into analysis: **Which specific choice addresses which plausible concern, and how does that serve the purpose?** Do not assume all readers respond identically or invent demographic details without evidence.

## Different kinds of infographic

- **Statistical:** inspect quantities, units, denominators, time periods, scales and sources. Ask whether the headline overstates the data.
- **Process or timeline:** inspect sequence, stages, arrows, dates and gaps. Ask what is made to seem simple or inevitable.
- **Comparison:** inspect matched categories and visual alignment. Ask whether the comparison is like for like.
- **Instruction or explainer:** inspect labels, grouping, examples, thresholds and calls to action. Ask how information becomes usable.

A single text may combine several of these approaches. Choose what to examine according to what the infographic needs to explain or persuade readers to do.

## A practical reading method

1. Establish the subject, context and likely purpose before listing techniques.
2. Identify the audience using details from the text and any supplied context.
3. Trace the overall argument or suggested reading path.
4. Select two or three significant relationships between words, images, numbers and arrangement.
5. Explain how those choices shape meaning for that audience. Check qualifications, omissions and alternative readings.

A strong response explains the combination: what does the wording clarify about the picture, or the arrangement imply about the information? Avoid organising an entire essay as an inventory of colours, fonts and devices.

## Vocabulary and further guidance

Useful starting terms include **salience, visual hierarchy, reading path, grouping, pictogram, anchorage, contrast, qualification, imperative** and **ethos**. Use a term only when it makes your explanation more precise.

- [Literary, rhetorical and image-analysis reference](/resources/analysis-reference)
- [Analytical verbs, tone words and sentence stems](/resources/analytical-language)
- [Language & Literature Paper 1](/courses/language-literature/assessment/c621c061-5e55-46a6-91b1-82f356b67a3d)
- [Purdue OWL: analysing visual documents](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/general_writing/visual_rhetoric/analyzing_visual_documents/index.html)

## Worked example

## Start here

Apply the overview to one complete infographic. Follow the relationship between its words, images and arrangement, then test your own reading against specific details.

### The text

**Physical activity for early years (2019)** is a public-health infographic issued by the UK Department of Health and Social Care. It translates recommendations into benefits, daily targets and activities. The source panel preserves the 2019 design; the current government download has been revised.

**Practice guiding question:** How do words and visual choices make the advice feel both authoritative and achievable?

First, look at the whole infographic without reading the model. What stands out? What does it ask someone to do? Use the close-up buttons beside the source to check small details. An initial reading might be: *the infographic presents children's activity as worthwhile, measurable and possible through ordinary play.* Treat that as a claim to test.

Work through **Audience and purpose → Read the design → Build a response**. Use **Vocabulary in action** to name relevant choices, and return to the Overview when meeting another infographic. The final section gives you a place to write and export your own analysis.

## Audience and purpose

### 1. Separate the subject from the audience

The subject is young children's activity. That does not make young children the principal readers. Adults usually arrange the activities and interpret the daily targets. The small explanatory labels and references to age groups support a reading aimed at **parents, caregivers and early-years practitioners**.

The [government publication page](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/physical-activity-guidelines-early-years-under-5s) also identifies **health professionals** as users of the resource when explaining activity. That is supplied context. Our inference about caregivers comes from what the text asks readers to understand and do. Distinguish these two kinds of evidence.

### 2. Ask what this audience values or needs

The benefits include sleep, social skills, health and readiness for school. Those are plausible adult concerns. The mix allows different readers to find a reason to value activity: a parent may notice sleep; a practitioner may notice learning and coordination. These are possibilities supported by the wording, not facts about every reader.

Do not invent a precise age, income, gender or family situation for the audience without evidence. “Mothers aged 25–40” is less defensible than “adults responsible for young children's routines.”

### 3. Turn the inference into analysis

Naming an audience is only the beginning. Connect **a reader's likely concern → a specific choice → the purpose it serves**.

- **Observation:** the introduction promises that active children “sleep better.”
- **Audience inference:** caregivers may value benefits that affect everyday routines as well as long-term health.
- **Analytical move:** By including sleep among the benefits, the infographic makes activity relevant to daily care, giving adults a practical reason to adopt its recommendations.

### 4. State a purpose as an action or change

“Inform people about exercise” is broad. Here, the text seeks to **encourage adults to provide regular, age-appropriate movement by making the recommendation understandable and manageable**. Informing and persuading can work together: the numerical target clarifies the advice, while the benefits and activity choices make acting on it more attractive.

Useful sentence stem: **For readers who need to ___, the combination of ___ and ___ presents ___ as ___.** Fill it with evidence; remove the frame if it makes the sentence awkward.

## Read the design

### 1. Benefits make the target worth considering

The six small benefit panels combine familiar icons with brief labels. The heart's label narrows its meaning toward health and weight; the building blocks connect play with learning. This is **image–text anchorage**: words help direct the interpretation of an image.

The repeated panels create **grouping**, making several benefits easy to scan. Their effect depends on their content: they present activity as contributing to several aspects of a child's life, rather than only physical strength. That gives adult readers several possible motivations.

### 2. A number becomes a memorable instruction

The large orange clock and oversized **180** create **salience**: they stand out through scale and contrast. The clock's familiar shape connects the recommendation with daily time. This is an **iconic representation of time**, not a pie chart showing proportions.

Read the surrounding words as carefully as the number. **“At least”** qualifies the target as a minimum; **“per day”** establishes frequency; **“for children 1–5 years”** identifies the group. These details prevent the large figure from becoming a universal instruction for every child. The separate Under-1s panel makes the age distinction visible.

### 3. The activity tiles make the instruction feel possible

The teal tiles offer a range of named actions, including walking, dancing, messy play and playground activity. Their repeated format creates **visual consistency** and presents them as related possibilities. The short labels anchor the simplified **pictograms**.

Read these tiles beside **“Every movement counts.”** The inclusive “every” and the variety of everyday actions widen what can count as activity. The combination can make the substantial daily target seem achievable through familiar routines. Do not assume the stepped arrangement is a developmental sequence: no arrows or age labels establish that reading.

### 4. The ending combines encouragement with authority

**“Get Strong. Move More. Break up inactivity”** uses three short **imperatives**. The parallel commands give the ending a brisk rhythm and leave the reader with actions to remember. The tone is directive but also encouraging, especially after the page has supplied examples of what to do.

The source line naming the UK Chief Medical Officers establishes **institutional authority**, or **ethos**. It gives readers a reason to regard the advice as medically informed. It does not, by itself, display the underlying studies or prove that every recommendation has been demonstrated on this page.

### Put the parts together

A possible reading path is **reasons → target → practical options → call to action**. The eye may instead go straight to the orange clock. Describe the hierarchy and relationships the design makes available, rather than claiming every reader follows one route.

## Build a response

### A possible thesis

By pairing a conspicuous daily target with familiar forms of play and an authoritative medical source, the infographic presents regular movement as both a serious responsibility and a manageable part of caring for young children.

This answers the practice question with an interpretation. It gives the response something to demonstrate; it does not simply promise paragraphs about colour, numbers and images.

### A plan organised around meaning

1. **Make activity matter:** connect the benefit labels and icons to adult concerns about care and development.
2. **Make the recommendation usable:** examine the prominent number, its qualifying language and the separate age groups.
3. **Make action feel achievable:** connect the activity tiles, the inclusive slogan and the closing commands.

Bring language and visual choices together within each idea. Select enough evidence to develop a reading; you do not need to mention every tile.

### Worked analytical paragraph

The infographic makes a demanding daily target appear manageable by placing the dominant orange clock beside a collection of ordinary activities. Although the oversized “180” gives the recommendation weight, the repeated tiles for walking, dancing and messy play show readers familiar ways of acting on it. The accompanying statement “Every movement counts” reinforces that breadth: “every” values small and varied forms of movement rather than reserving activity for organised sport. For adults arranging a child's day, this pairing can recast an abstract time requirement as a set of practical choices. The design therefore supports its public-health purpose through a combination of numerical emphasis and reassurance.

### Why this develops analysis

- **Interpretation:** the opening proposes a relationship between a demanding target and manageable action.
- **Evidence:** the paragraph names visible features and quotes wording that actually appears.
- **Explanation:** it connects the tiles to the breadth of “every.” It goes beyond naming colour or listing activities.
- **Audience and purpose:** it explains why that relationship could matter to adults organising care.
- **Evaluation:** it judges the contribution of the combined choices to the larger purpose. It does not guarantee compliance or claim a mark for the paragraph.

This is one defensible reading. Another response could examine whether the very prominent number overshadows the smaller qualifications. Support that judgement with the relative size and placement of those details.

[Develop an introduction](/resources/paper-1-introductions?example=language-literature) or practise the movement [from observation to analysis](/resources/observation-to-analysis).

## Vocabulary in action

Use a term to make an observation more precise. Follow it with evidence and interpretation; the terminology is not the analysis.

### Attention and organisation

- **Salience:** how much an element stands out. *The orange clock gives the daily target greater salience than the source line.*
- **Visual hierarchy:** the ordering of attention through size, position and contrast. *The hierarchy foregrounds the target before readers inspect its qualifications.*
- **Reading path:** a route the design suggests through its elements. *The movement from benefits to activities links motivation with action.*
- **Grouping / proximity:** placing items together so they appear connected. *Repeated tiles group varied actions as possible forms of movement.*
- **Contrast:** a difference that distinguishes elements. *Orange separates the target and infant guidance from the teal activity tiles.*
- **Typography:** the treatment of lettering, including size and weight. *The bold numeral makes the recommendation conspicuous; its smaller surrounding words specify its scope.*

### Words, images and persuasion

- **Pictogram:** a simplified picture representing an object or action. *The walking pictogram makes an ordinary activity recognisable at a glance.*
- **Anchorage:** wording that directs how an image is understood. *The health-and-weight label narrows the heart icon's possible meanings.*
- **Imperative:** a grammatical command. *The closing imperatives turn the explanation into a prompt to act.*
- **Qualification:** wording that limits or specifies a claim. *“At least” defines a minimum rather than an exact or maximum duration.*
- **Register:** language suited to a situation and audience. *Everyday activity labels create an accessible register within an official publication.*
- **Ethos:** an appeal to credibility or authority. *The named medical officers lend institutional credibility to the advice.*

### When there is a statistical chart

**Encoding** is how a visible feature represents information: bar length might represent a count. A **legend** explains a code, while an **axis**, **baseline** and **unit** establish how quantities should be read. **Proportion** describes a part in relation to a whole. Those terms are useful for actual data displays; the clock in our example does not plot a distribution.

### Verbs that do analytical work

**Foregrounds** draws attention to something; **groups** establishes a relationship; **qualifies** sets a limit; **anchors** directs a reading; **contrasts** distinguishes; **translates** makes an abstraction more concrete; **positions** invites a reader toward a stance; **legitimises** presents something as credible or acceptable.

Try: **The [precise choice] foregrounds/qualifies/translates ___, inviting [supported audience] to understand ___ as ___.** Use a cautious verb when the effect cannot be guaranteed. See [analytical verbs and tone vocabulary](/resources/analytical-language) for a wider bank.

## Avoid and revise

### Naming instead of explaining

**Thin:** “The bright colour grabs attention.”

**Developed:** “The orange target contrasts with the teal activity tiles, making the daily recommendation conspicuous while visually separating it from the menu of ways to meet it.”

### Guessing an audience

**Thin:** “It is for children because there are cartoons.”

**Developed:** “Although the pictograms depict play, the age-specific targets and references to school readiness address adults who plan young children's routines.”

### Turning a possibility into a certainty

**Thin:** “The pictures make every parent exercise with their child.”

**Developed:** “The familiar activities can make the recommendation appear feasible for caregivers, although the page cannot establish how readers will act.”

### Misreading what a number does

**Incorrect:** “The pie chart proves that children spend 180 minutes exercising.”

**Accurate:** “The clock-shaped callout presents a recommended minimum. It does not report observed behaviour or divide a whole into proportions.”

### Treating colour as a fixed code

Do not assume orange always means energy or teal always means health. Begin with how the colours distinguish, group or emphasise elements in this particular design. A symbolic interpretation needs additional support.

## Practice and transfer

### Before looking at the model again

Choose one relationship: **benefit icons and labels**, **the number and its qualifications**, or **the activity tiles and the slogan**. Explain how that relationship shapes the message for an audience you can support with evidence. Use the writing space below.

### Transfer the method

On your next infographic, record its purpose, the audience evidence and what it needs to explain or persuade readers to do before choosing terminology. Then ask which features actually matter. An infographic explaining a process may require a reading of sequence; a charity infographic may require scrutiny of statistics and a donation appeal. Reuse the questions, not a paragraph plan designed for a different text.

For a full response, return to [Language & Literature Paper 1](/courses/language-literature/assessment/c621c061-5e55-46a6-91b1-82f356b67a3d). For another explanation of visual analysis, see [Purdue OWL: analysing visual documents](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/general_writing/visual_rhetoric/analyzing_visual_documents/index.html).

items.title: Advertisement
items.summary: Read how advertisements build a preference through audience appeals, language and design. Explore a separate FIJI Water worked example.
items.body:
## What advertisements do

An advertisement is a designed message that promotes a product, service, organisation, cause or behaviour. It selects what an audience sees and how they encounter it, making a particular response seem desirable, necessary or possible. That response might be buying, donating, signing up, remembering a brand or changing a habit.

Commercial advertising often connects a purchase with a wider promise: convenience, confidence, belonging, status or pleasure. A public-service advertisement may instead ask the audience to avoid a risk or act for others. Both can combine information with persuasion. Start by asking **what is being offered or urged, to whom, and on what grounds**.

This guide concentrates on print and static digital advertisements. In video or audio advertising, also examine movement, editing, voice, music and timing. The central task stays the same: explain how the choices work together to shape a message for an audience.

## Audience, purpose and appeals

The person shown in an advertisement is not automatically its target reader. Infer the audience from the need or desire addressed, the language, the assumed knowledge, the action requested and any supplied publication context. Separate evidence from guesses about age, income or identity.

Then connect a plausible audience concern with a specific choice:

- **Desire and aspiration:** What kind of life, identity or experience is made attractive? How is it linked to the product or action?
- **Fear, care and responsibility:** What seems at risk, and whose wellbeing is involved? Does the ad offer a way to act on that emotion?
- **Belonging and distinction:** Who is presented as “us,” admirable or successful? Does the audience gain acceptance by joining a group, or status by standing apart?
- **Credibility and trust:** Whose voice supports the message, and why might this audience value that voice?
- **Reason and practicality:** What evidence, benefit, saving or solution makes the proposal appear sensible? What assumptions does that reasoning depend on?
- **Agency:** How do wording and practical details make the response seem within reach?

Ethos, pathos and logos can help you describe an appeal, but they are **not a ready-made three-part thesis or paragraph plan**. Organise your response around what the advertisement is doing.

- **Pathos:** name the particular emotion—fear, tenderness, guilt, pride, reassurance—and explain how the choices evoke it for this audience. “The baby creates pathos” leaves the analysis unfinished; explain how its presentation invites, for example, protective concern and why that matters to the appeal.
- **Ethos:** explain how credibility is established. A text can draw on existing reputation or expertise, but can also build trust through its voice, apparent knowledge, candour or attention to the audience’s concerns.
- **Logos:** explain the reasoning: how does evidence, a comparison or a cause-and-effect claim support a conclusion? A number alone is not an explanation of logos. Ask what it is used to demonstrate and whether that inference is justified.

The appeals often work together within a single persuasive move. A precise explanation matters more than including all three labels.

State the purpose as a change: **the advertisement invites this audience to see ___ as ___ and to respond by ___.** The desired response is not evidence that the campaign succeeded. You can evaluate how well choices support the message without inventing audience reactions or sales figures.

## Common features and techniques

These are possibilities to investigate, not a checklist every advertisement must satisfy.

### Headline, slogan and body copy

The headline usually offers an entry point: a promise, question, challenge or surprising claim. A slogan is a short, repeatable phrase associated with a brand or campaign; it is not simply any large sentence. Body copy develops the message through explanation, testimony, evidence or an offer.

**Possible analysis:** A concise headline may make a claim memorable while smaller copy qualifies it. A question can invite readers to recognise a need; a double meaning can make an image take on new significance. Explain the particular promise or tension, rather than saying that large type “grabs attention.”

### Image and wording

Photographs, illustrations, objects and settings can demonstrate a benefit, embody a risk or associate a product with a way of life. Notice framing, gaze, posture, scale, angle and what has been left outside the frame.

**Possible analysis:** Wording can anchor an image by directing its interpretation. Alternatively, the image may complete a verbal joke, challenge a claim or reveal a consequence. Ask what meaning the combination creates that either part would leave incomplete. A person looking towards the camera can create a sense of address; the surrounding expression and wording determine whether that encounter seems inviting, confrontational or intimate.

### Layout, colour and typography

Relative size, placement, contrast and empty space establish visual hierarchy. Proximity can connect a claim with a product, an image with its caption, or an offer with a response button. Repeated colours and lettering can make a campaign recognisable.

**Possible analysis:** A large image may establish an emotional encounter before smaller copy supplies a reason to act. A restrained layout may associate a brand with exclusivity; a crowded arrangement may emphasise abundance or urgency. Test those readings against the actual wording and design. Colours do not carry one fixed meaning across all advertisements.

### Brand, testimony and evidence

Brand logos identify who stands behind the message. A named customer, expert or campaign participant can supply a voice with a particular kind of credibility. Figures, demonstrations and comparisons can make benefits or risks seem concrete.

**Possible analysis:** Distinguish institutional authority, relevant expertise, celebrity appeal and personal experience. Ask what each source is qualified to support. Examine the scope of a statistic or comparison: a precise-looking number is not, by itself, a strong argument. A photograph presents a selected view of reality, even when its subject is a real person.

### Call to action and small print

A call to action tells the audience what to do next: call, visit, buy, join, donate or try. Contact details, links, prices and deadlines can make a response easier or more urgent. Small print may limit an offer or qualify a prominent claim.

**Possible analysis:** Connect the action to the preceding appeal. Does the ad supply an achievable response to a problem it has raised? Does a deadline create pressure? Does smaller wording change the meaning of the headline? Some brand advertisements aim chiefly to build recognition or association and contain no immediate instruction.

## Different advertising situations

- **Product or service advertising:** distinguish the practical benefit from the identity or feeling attached to it. Examine how the offer and its conditions fit together.
- **Brand advertising:** look for recurring associations, values and recognisable design. A memorable image may do more work than a direct sales instruction.
- **Public-service or advocacy advertising:** identify the behaviour or attitude being promoted. Consider the relationship between warning, testimony, responsibility and support.
- **Sponsored or native content:** examine how commercial purpose is disclosed and how editorial, personal or informational styles contribute to credibility.

Categories overlap. A charity appeal may use the form of an advertisement, letter or video. A publisher or platform is a source of context, not a text type. Use the features of the actual text to decide which questions are productive.

## A practical reading method

1. **Orient:** identify the advertiser, subject, medium and supplied context. Separate the organisation publishing the message from any person speaking within it.
2. **Infer:** identify the likely audience, the concern being addressed and the proposed response. Name the details that support those inferences.
3. **Survey:** trace the hierarchy and a plausible reading path. Where do attention, tone or emphasis shift? Readers need not follow one fixed route.
4. **Connect:** choose two or three significant relationships between wording, image and arrangement. Explain how each combination develops the appeal.
5. **Construct:** build a thesis about the ad’s persuasive logic. Organise paragraphs around meanings or moves, such as creating a need, making a promise and offering a response.
6. **Verify:** check quotations, visual details, qualifications and claims about the audience. Distinguish what the text shows from what you infer.

Before writing, try this two-sentence task: **What does the advertisement invite its audience to believe or do? How does one precise relationship between words and image support that invitation?** If the second sentence could describe almost any ad, return to the source.

## Vocabulary and further guidance

Use **headline, slogan, body copy** and **call to action** to identify parts of the message; **salience, visual hierarchy, framing, gaze** and **anchorage** to describe relationships; and **direct address, imperative, connotation, metaphor, contrast, testimony** and **appeal** where they clarify a choice. A label starts an explanation; it does not complete it.

- [Literary, rhetorical and image-analysis reference](/resources/analysis-reference)
- [Analytical verbs, tone words and sentence stems](/resources/analytical-language)
- [SOAPSTone: a rhetorical reading scaffold](/courses/language-literature/resources/eab78d37-cc35-476e-a70b-d1b674c8f512)
- [Language & Literature Paper 1](/courses/language-literature/assessment/c621c061-5e55-46a6-91b1-82f356b67a3d)

## Worked example

## Start with the whole advertisement

This FIJI Water advertisement builds a contrast between an unnamed alternative and its own branded bottle. The supplied source is a wide print-ad scan. Begin with the whole composition, then follow **Orient → Analyse → Write**. Each section pairs the commentary with a useful source view. You can switch to the whole ad or another detail at any point, or enlarge the source for a closer look.

Before reading the model, explain what each side of the spread asks you to associate with bottled water. A reading to test is: **the advertisement creates anxiety about artificial intervention, then presents the named product as a reassuring, natural alternative.**

The commentary and practice question are original teaching material. The publication date, original placement and photographer are not identified in the supplied scan. Analyse the claims as advertising claims; the image does not establish how competing water is produced.

## Audience and purpose

The advertisement addresses potential bottled-water buyers who value a product presented as clean, natural and healthy. The closing reference to refreshment supports that inference. The explanatory copy assumes that distance from pollution and protection underground will matter to the reader’s judgement of quality.

Avoid inventing an exact age, income or nationality for the audience. There is no price, retailer or publication context in the supplied ad to establish those details. Instead, connect the audience’s plausible concern about what they consume with the ad’s contrast between interference and protection.

The purpose is to **make FIJI Water seem preferable to competing bottled water and encourage readers to choose it**. This is not a neutral explanation of water production: the copy develops a comparison and ends with a purchasing invitation. Its argument combines an unsettling image, a reassuring product claim and an account of natural protection.

## 1. The image creates the problem

[Zoom into the syringe and unbranded bottle](#ad-view-syringe).

The left side gives a large area to a gloved hand holding a syringe beside an open, unbranded bottle. The needle points into the bottle’s silhouette. The harsh lighting and dark background make the action seem suspicious, rather than an ordinary scene of drinking or refreshment.

The glove and syringe carry clinical or laboratory associations. In another context, they could suggest care or precision. Here, the contrast with the headline and the clean presentation of the branded product directs those associations towards unwanted interference. That is **anchorage**: words help determine how the visual detail is read.

**Pathos — fear and unease:** the syringe can make an ordinary purchase feel potentially risky. The appeal addresses concern about what enters the body; the branded side then offers reassurance. Explain that emotional movement rather than claiming every reader will be frightened.

The large bottle makes the unnamed alternative conspicuous, but prominence does not make it desirable. The advertisement uses **salience** to establish a problem before offering a product. The unbranded bottle also allows a broad comparison: it can stand for other bottled water without identifying a specific competitor.

Do not write that the photograph proves competitors inject harmful substances into their bottles. It makes that suspicion vivid. A stronger analytical claim explains how the ad suggests that idea and why it might matter to a concerned buyer.

## 2. The headline supplies the distinction

[Zoom into the headline](#ad-view-headline).

**“Fiji Water. No Added Chemicals.”** names the product and immediately supplies its distinguishing claim. The short, separate statements make the claim sound definite. The negative “No” defines the brand through the absence of something the adjacent syringe encourages readers to fear.

Read the headline across the spread. The left image supplies a disturbing version of addition; the right wording offers the named product as its opposite. Without the words, the syringe’s purpose would be more ambiguous. Without the image, the claim would lose much of its visual threat. The persuasion depends on that relationship.

The contrast between the dark photograph and the open white space on the right makes the branded side appear comparatively clear and controlled. This is an effect of the arrangement here, not a rule that white always means purity. Blue appears on both bottles, so the argument is more precise when it examines lighting, framing, labelling and surrounding space together.

## 3. The copy gives reassurance a rationale

[Zoom into the body copy](#ad-view-copy).

The opening distinguishes “Other water” from “Our water.” The repeated contrast establishes two camps before the copy explains the brand’s claimed advantage. Its account of an artesian aquifer, distance from pollution and layers of clay and rock gives natural protection a concrete setting.

Words describing the source as deep underground and the route into the bottle as direct make the journey seem protected and uninterrupted. The list of pollution, acid rain and industrial waste builds a picture of environmental danger; the account of clay and rock supplies a barrier against it. The explanation turns the headline’s reassurance into an apparently reasoned product story.

**Logos — a proposed reason to prefer the product:** the copy links a protected source and direct bottling with the conclusion that FIJI is a better choice. Evaluate that chain of reasoning and the evidence it provides, not just the presence of explanation.

The technical term **“artesian aquifer”** creates a specialised register—a style of language associated with expert knowledge. This contributes to **ethos**, an appeal to credibility: the brand builds an informed, knowledgeable voice rather than relying only on an established reputation. There is no named independent expert or study in the displayed ad. Technical language can make the account sound authoritative, but does not itself verify the comparison. Likewise, the exclusivity claim that FIJI is the only bottled water with the stated protection asserts an advantage without supplying comparative evidence within this ad.

Notice a shift in scope: the headline refers to **added** chemicals, while the opening copy makes the broader claim **“free of chemicals.”** Water itself is a chemical substance. In this context, the ad encourages readers to associate the word with undesirable contaminants. Distinguishing the connotation from the literal meaning helps evaluate the rhetoric without adopting its wording as scientific fact.

## 4. The product and slogan resolve the contrast

[Zoom into the FIJI bottle](#ad-view-product), then [inspect the closing slogan](#ad-view-slogan).

The smaller branded bottle is isolated against the light background. Its recognisable name and leafy, floral label give readers a specific product to choose, in contrast with the anonymous bottle on the left. The plant imagery reinforces the natural associations developed in the copy; it is not evidence of the water’s composition or environmental impact.

The slogan **“Natural. Clean. Pure. Fiji.”** uses short fragments and repeated full stops to present three desirable qualities as a sequence. Ending that sequence with the brand name encourages the reader to carry those qualities into the final word. FIJI becomes the resolution of the contrast established across the spread.

The body copy also invites the reader to **“treat yourself.”** That phrasing makes the choice sound like a small act of care or pleasure. There is no price, deadline or immediate ordering instruction in the displayed ad. The invitation is to favour the brand on a later buying occasion, rather than respond to a limited-time offer.

### How the appeals work together

The fear appeal gives readers a reason to worry; the account of natural protection offers a reason to trust the alternative; the informed voice makes that account sound credible. The light setting, plant imagery and positive slogan supply reassurance. **Pathos, logos and ethos help explain the same persuasive movement.** They do not supply a three-part thesis or essay plan. Keep the argument centred on how the ad turns concern about an alternative into preference for the brand.

### Put the spread back together

Switch the source to **Whole ad**. One plausible movement is **unease → distinction → explanation → desirable choice**. Another reader might start with the headline. The interpretation does not depend on everyone following a fixed route: the two sides remain in a relationship of contrast, and the headline, copy, product and slogan reinforce it.

## Build an analytical response

### A possible thesis

By contrasting a syringe beside an anonymous bottle with an isolated, recognisable product, the advertisement frames other bottled water as vulnerable to interference and FIJI as a reassuring natural choice; its explanatory copy and compressed closing slogan develop that preference into a reason to buy.

This answers the practice question with a persuasive relationship. It does not merely announce that the ad uses images, colour and language.

### A plan organised around meaning

1. **Create doubt about the alternative:** connect the syringe, the unbranded bottle, the dramatic lighting and the opening comparison.
2. **Make the brand’s difference seem credible:** connect the headline’s negative claim with the account of source, distance and natural protection.
3. **Turn reassurance into preference:** connect the isolated product, the plant imagery, the slogan’s sequence and the invitation to treat oneself.

These are possible lines of argument, not three compulsory paragraphs. Bring language and visual choices together within each idea.

### Worked analytical paragraph

The advertisement makes FIJI Water appear reassuring by first constructing an unsettling alternative. On the left, the gloved hand and syringe beside an unbranded bottle give the idea of addition a clinical, intrusive form. The headline’s “No Added Chemicals” then anchors the image: it directs readers to see the syringe as adding something unwanted and FIJI as free from that interference. Against the dark photograph, the light space surrounding the smaller FIJI bottle offers a visual form of the same reassurance. The contrast invites buyers concerned about what they consume to associate the anonymous alternative with interference and the branded product with protection. Its force comes from the combination of image and claim, although the staged visual comparison does not itself establish the quality of competing waters.

### What the reasoning does

- Proposes a meaning: reassurance depends on an unsettling alternative.
- Locates specific visual details and quotes the relevant wording.
- Explains how the headline directs the reading of the image.
- Connects the contrast with an audience concern supported by the text.
- Evaluates the strategy while distinguishing suggestion from proof.

Use the [Paper 1 guide](/courses/language-literature/assessment/c621c061-5e55-46a6-91b1-82f356b67a3d) for the wider reading and writing method. Becky’s CDC example there demonstrates a different persuasive situation: a public-health call to change behaviour. It remains a separate assessment example.

## Avoid and revise

**Thin:** “Blue makes the audience feel calm and want to buy the water.”

**Developed:** “Because blue appears in both bottles, the more significant distinction is between the dark, intrusive syringe image and the clearly labelled product isolated against white.”

**Thin:** “The image proves that other companies add dangerous chemicals.”

**Developed:** “The syringe dramatises artificial intervention, while the headline encourages readers to treat FIJI as an exception; the ad supplies an association rather than proof of competitors’ practices.”

**Thin:** “The target audience is rich adults aged 30–50.”

**Developed:** “The emphasis on protection from pollution and the closing reference to healthy refreshment address bottled-water buyers concerned about quality.”

Avoid treating the model as either a scientific product review or a list of tricks. Explain how the particular wording and design build a preference, then evaluate the support and limits of that argument.

## Practice and transfer

Choose the body copy or the closing slogan. Write a short paragraph explaining how its language develops the visual contrast. Include one precise phrase, one visual detail and a connection to audience or purpose. The writing space below gives you a place to try this before returning to the model.

For another advertisement, begin again with its actual offer and evidence. A luxury brand might sell distinction without explaining production; a charity appeal might connect an individual story with a donation request. Reuse the questions about audience, image–text relationships and desired response. Do not assume every ad uses FIJI’s opposition between interference and nature.

items.title: Charitable appeal
items.summary: Explore how appeals connect need, trust and participation, then follow a separate WWF adoption example.
items.body:
## What a charitable appeal does

A charitable appeal asks an audience to contribute to a cause: money, time, goods, expertise or public support. It connects a need with a possible response and gives the reader a reason to participate. Its central task is to make a contribution seem **worthwhile, credible and within reach**.

The cause might involve disaster relief, conservation, medical research, housing, education or a local community project. Some appeals demand an immediate response to a crisis. Others invite a lasting relationship through regular giving, membership, sponsorship or symbolic adoption. An appeal can draw on solidarity, admiration, hope or a sense of justice as well as concern about suffering.

“Charitable appeal” names what a text is trying to do. It can take several forms: an advertisement, letter, email, speech, leaflet or donation webpage. Name the form when it matters. A personal letter can develop a sustained voice and relationship; a webpage can combine a story with donation options, photographs and expandable explanations. Analyse the text in front of you rather than expecting one fixed layout.

## Audience, purpose and the reader’s role

Distinguish **who speaks, who is addressed and who or what benefits**. A charity may speak through a campaign team, a researcher, a volunteer or a person describing their own experience. The intended donor is not necessarily the person pictured. The organisation usually acts as an intermediary: it receives contributions and arranges or carries out the promised work.

Infer the audience from the request, medium, assumed values and knowledge, and any supplied context. A renewal letter addresses a different relationship from a first appeal. A gift adoption may address both the purchaser and the eventual recipient. A small recurring payment can suggest an accessible commitment without proving the reader’s income, age or occupation.

Ask what role the appeal offers its reader. Are they invited to be a neighbour, partner, witness, protector, member of a movement or supporter of specialist work? Direct address can make a distant issue personally relevant; inclusive pronouns can make action feel shared. Check who is included in “we” and what “you” is being asked to take responsibility for.

State the purpose precisely: **the appeal invites this audience to support ___ by ___, presenting that contribution as ___.** “To raise awareness” is incomplete if the text also asks for a donation or regular commitment. The invitation is evidence of the intended response, not proof that readers actually gave.

## How the appeal builds its case

The following are common persuasive moves, not compulsory sections or a paragraph template. They may overlap, repeat or appear in a different order.

### Make the need matter

An appeal can bring a large issue into focus through a particular person, animal, place or event. A name, a short narrative, a quotation or a photograph can make the subject recognisable. Wider figures can then establish scale. Examine how the individual example relates to the broader problem: what does it help the reader understand, and what can it reasonably represent?

**Possible analysis:** A movement from one account to a wider figure can connect personal concern with collective need. A contrast between what exists now and what might be lost can create urgency. Explain the particular relationship; the presence of a child or an animal does not, by itself, explain an emotional appeal.

### Show that a response is possible

Concern becomes a case for giving when the appeal explains what action could change. Look for a connection between the problem, the proposed work and the contribution. Concrete actions can make an abstract promise easier to imagine. A progress story may establish that change has already begun and invite the reader to help continue it.

**Possible analysis:** A sequence from need to practical intervention can turn distress into hope or determination. Notice the force of verbs such as “can,” “could” and “will”: an illustration of possible impact differs from a guarantee. If a donation amount is paired with an outcome, examine the unit, timescale and qualifications before describing what the money achieves.

### Establish confidence in the organisation

An appeal may draw on a known name, relevant expertise, partnerships, testimony or evidence of previous work. It can also build credibility through specific explanations, an informed voice and a clear account of how contributions are used. A logo identifies the organisation; explain what makes its authority relevant to this request.

**Possible analysis:** Naming an intervention and the people who carry it out can make the organisation appear capable of translating concern into action. An explanation of funding can reassure a reader about the scope of the promise. Identify the evidence supplied by the text and distinguish it from an independent assessment of the charity.

### Make participation feel achievable

The call to action names a next step: donate, volunteer, sponsor, join, give supplies or share a campaign. Donation options, contact details, deadlines and a simple response form can reduce uncertainty about how to participate. A recurring amount frames support as an ongoing relationship; a one-off request may respond to a particular moment.

**Possible analysis:** Breaking a commitment into monthly payments can make it easier to envisage within a budget. A suggested amount also gives readers a reference point for deciding what to contribute. Examine both the apparent ease of the first step and the actual commitment being requested.

### Sustain a relationship

Thank-you messages, updates, membership language, certificates and gifts can give participation a continuing presence in the donor’s life. A symbolic adoption can make support for a species feel like a personal connection. The appeal may offer recognition, belonging or satisfaction alongside its stated charitable outcome.

**Possible analysis:** A tangible reminder can connect an otherwise distant project with everyday experience. Ask how that benefit supports the appeal and how the wording explains its relationship to the cause. A benefit to the donor does not automatically invalidate the charitable purpose.

## Language, image and design

Read the wording and presentation together. A photograph can establish an encounter that a headline interprets; a caption can identify someone as a participant with knowledge and agency, or present them chiefly through their need. Gaze, distance, setting and posture matter because of the relationship they construct here, not because every close-up or direct gaze has one fixed effect.

Notice the hierarchy between the story, evidence and response. A large donation button may keep action visible while the reader considers the explanation. Repeated requests can provide several opportunities to respond. Smaller qualifications can change the scope of a prominent promise. On a webpage, placement, links and interactive controls are part of the text’s organisation.

Examine diction, pronouns, modality, questions, imperatives, repetition and contrasts. Urgent language may stress the consequences of delay; a calm, specific explanation may make complicated work seem manageable. A conversational voice may establish familiarity, while a specialised register may suggest expertise. Connect the choice to the audience’s concern or the organisation’s proposed response.

Ethos, pathos and logos can describe parts of this work, but **do not use them as a default three-part thesis**. For pathos, name the emotion and show how it is constructed. For ethos, explain how credibility is built or drawn upon. For logos, trace the reasoning from need through intervention to likely benefit. A sad subject, a logo or a number leaves the explanation unfinished.

## Different situations and questions of representation

- **Emergency appeals:** examine the relationship between immediate danger, the time available and the proposed response. Distinguish a specific deadline from a general sense of urgency.
- **Long-term giving and research:** examine how the appeal makes sustained or uncertain work meaningful. Progress, patience and collective contribution may matter more than a rapid solution.
- **Conservation and symbolic adoption:** examine how a species, habitat or individual animal becomes a focus for support, and how a personal relationship connects with wider work.
- **Local and community appeals:** examine shared place, experience and responsibility. The reader may already know the people involved or benefit from the project themselves.

Ask whose voice and agency the appeal makes visible. Do people speak about their own circumstances? What role do local knowledge, collective action or specialist work play? Does the reader appear as one contributor among others or as the sole source of change? Support your answer with the actual choices. Emotional force is not automatically manipulation, and an appeal need not explain every cause of a problem to make a specific request.

## A practical reading method

1. **Orient:** identify the organisation, cause, form and supplied context. Locate the exact contribution requested.
2. **Infer:** identify the likely reader and the values, concerns or existing relationship the appeal addresses.
3. **Trace:** follow how the text connects need, possible change and participation. Notice where it establishes trust or answers a likely hesitation.
4. **Connect:** select precise relationships between language, images, evidence and the response mechanism.
5. **Evaluate:** check the scale and terms of the promise. Separate what the appeal shows, what it claims and what you infer.
6. **Construct:** organise an argument around the work the appeal does, such as making a distant need personal or turning concern into a manageable commitment.

Before writing, complete this thought: **The appeal makes ___ matter to ___, then presents ___ as a way to contribute because ___.** Return to the source wherever the connection is vague. These prompts support a reading; they are not a compulsory sequence for an essay.

## Vocabulary and further guidance

Useful terms include **direct address, inclusive pronouns, imperative, modality, testimony, narrative, framing, visual hierarchy, call to action** and **symbolic adoption**. Use **agency** to discuss who can act, **solidarity** for an invitation to shared responsibility, and **donor benefit** for something offered to the supporter. Explain the specific choice before adding a label.

- [Literary, rhetorical and image-analysis reference](/resources/analysis-reference)
- [Analytical verbs, tone words and sentence stems](/resources/analytical-language)
- [Advertisement: audience appeals, language and design](/courses/language-literature/text-types/cf482e4c-3555-4e12-afca-b63396aec3ea)
- [Language & Literature Paper 1](/courses/language-literature/assessment/c621c061-5e55-46a6-91b1-82f356b67a3d)

## Worked example

## Start with the appeal

This worked example examines WWF-UK’s snow-leopard adoption webpage, checked on 24 September 2026. It is an online fundraising appeal: the reader is invited to support conservation through a symbolic adoption. The source panel includes a small excerpt of its opening image and headline; open the complete WWF page to inspect the payment choices, gift images and supporting explanation in their original layout. A live page can change, so the notes identify the version examined here.
